newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian BASF slams high wage costs, taxes.
newsitem.headline: Belgian BASF slams high wage costs, taxes.

text.p: BASF Antwerpen NV, the Belgian production unit of German chemicals group BASF AG, on Wednesday attacked regional and federal governments for failing to act on high labour costs and what it called unreasonable taxation.

"Wage costs remain too high in comparison with the countries surrounding us," management board chairman Antoon Dieusaert told a news conference. "The gap becomes even bigger when we look at labour costs in, for example, Great Britain and Spain."
Dieusaert blamed costs which came on top of salaries and national contributions, particularly those for social security.

"We regret a social security reform remains bogged down in good intentions," he said, while admitting the government's room to move was limited by the need to curb Belgian state debt in line with the Maastricht Treaty on Europe's single currency.

He also attacked Belgium's complex collective bargaining system, where the buck was being passed with responsibility ending up with the government which was then forced to take sweeping measures instead of sector agreements being reached.

"In Belgium you sometimes have to talk to up to six different union partners, which results in nothing but a bidding war...this prevents creative and tailor-made solutions," he said. In the Netherlands and Germany employers frequently had to deal with only one partner.
"I fear the worst if we cannot succeed in making long-term deals." This was not an ultimatum, just "urgent advice", he said.

While moving production abroad was not a realistic option -- BASF Antwerpen operates on a six kilometre by six kilometre site with billions of francs of plant equipment -- the company could opt to temporarily shut operations and make some of its products elsewhere, Dieusaert said.

Delocalisation is a hot topic in Belgium since French car maker Renault decided last month to close its assembly plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels by July 1997 to reduce costs and overcapacity, costing 3,100 workers their jobs.
The work is being re-distributed to plants in France and Spain, where labour costs are lower.
In the car sector, to employ a Belgian worker costs 44.60 marks per hour, but only 28 marks in Spain and 27 marks in Britain.

BASF Antwerpen, which employed 3,600 people itself and had work for 1,600 workers at subcontractors in 1996, was currently conducting a study comparing labour costs in its sector with those in the Netherlands, France and Germany.
Total staff costs rose by 4.8 percent in 1996, with compensation for inflation accounting for just 1.7 percent.
Dieusaert said the company was also being pressured by taxes and levies which were unrelated to earnings.
He singled out an inflation-linked real estate tax which the company estimated would rise to one billion Belgian francs in three years' time from over half a billion at present.

Dieusaert said indexation made no sense for plant and equipment. "It is like a car...the value drops as you use it." So the government should take depreciation into account when taxing industrial installations.

A tax by the Flemish region on side products which BASF used as raw material and fuel also made little sense when taking into account government efforts to promote recycling and alternative energy sources.
Dieusaert noted burning some side products caused less pollution than burning ordinary fuels.
BASF Antwerpen reported an about one third fall in 1996 profit to 4.3 billion Belgian francs. It said this was mainly due to weak demand, low stock levels and rising raw material prices.
